e-8473.knowledge_point: Identifying the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Curve Using a Diagram
e-8473.problem:
Draw a diagram that depicts the lines representing the principal axes of the quadratic curve shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/5354b2fa6d2fb2c8b1b9ea3cb675225619e8debe64e1ec108b556248d6e672ec.png)
e-8473.worked_solution:
The principal axes of a curve define a coordinate system in which the curve can be represented by its (simplest) canonical equation. 

Our curve is a hyperbola. This curve will have the canonical equation of the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

if one axis passes through the vertices of the hyperbola and the other axis is the perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting the two vertices.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/bd0d117543012be1c4eab0acda878c9aea67518e46c93048e8c249de1a0c03e6.png)

e-8277.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2= 70?$
e-8277.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2.$ To  determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/33a30f2c07875359a60caed74f802a2de29ac9e44089800ed8f30a2015303bce.png)

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -70 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =7,\,-10\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $7y_1^2 -10 y_2^2.$  

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}-10{y}_{2}^{2} & =70 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{10}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{7} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{10})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{10}$ and $\sqrt{7}.$

e-8678.problem: Consider the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/4114e6536f57106949ed39a6ae4979646a0dd58c5690d7e7bcf9ffed15de8086.png) and the quadratic curve $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=1,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
e-8678.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/771d020606de64641ab305039a0c9a9de926080e83707b270a333b5775a8e028.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/54a77383e863630dfd4e21a796801001aaed3084f1097bca62ef4a098e20b405.png)

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/e0d71ad9216b9fa7c1831e6874b9a97bba9c1d9c5dbd6d9664635ed468d82a4c.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/83fd398b476c1c749346754a05c7f4071a98ab61453405a99ad8fcff65e38aaf.png)

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/8f0d84bb5c3ae37714c781b5dafbba1ae7de8561234ca558d3da2dcbfa9d75cf.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/293ad98697d595e3e0049aae93e54209b6d17aa92eb131b57791f211167690fc.png)

e-8276.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve
e-8276.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $19x_1^2-6x_1x_2+11x_2^2 = 20.$
e-8276.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=19x_1^2-6x_1x_2+11x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/31f8c54fecdb8b2e8b3f3cad20a642a39eab9ae2987d49849a1c1dabc34e5368.png)

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 20
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=20 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=10.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_2=20,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-20I & =[\begin{aligned}19 & -3 \\ -3 & 11\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-20I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/51897cac20d424f599eba1c8aada5259279ab9ad263e7557d6614ce79e68fa0f.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/f9913f9139af447be912bccc2350f086ce32bae89849495f8e82a3eebf8a7918.png)

- For $\lambda_1=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}19 & -3 \\ -3 & 11\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/2cdd8527be173b17e254bd4ecda571d71b15938c3a1f6cb2609122db2b10c64d.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/f6764ef3200afce932740e8100915018b6a0c21e902d932b218e79bcd57e0b95.png)

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/1549a73afb90f3fa0fb8218d9d63daa1a5534c3e546613cbf3f226371b8f1092.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/d4a6e3f0c138e6dd83252df8adc14359ba67ae77dec0270264ea6d00c7b08667.png)

Question 6
?

Which curve is defined by the equation 5x12+2x1x2+5x22=12?

a
 An ellipse with semiaxes 2 and 3
b
A hyperbola with semiaxes 3 and 2
c
A hyperbola with semiaxes 3 and 2
d
 An ellipse with semiaxes 1 and 2
e
A circle of radius 2
Submit

decision.explanation: The quadratic-form matrix is [[5,1],[1,5]], with eigenvalues 6 and 4. In orthonormal principal coordinates, the equation becomes 6y₁²+4y₂²=12, or y₁²/2+y₂²/3=1. Thus it is an ellipse with semiaxes √2 and √3.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $5{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}=12?$
after.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=5{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +24 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =6,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $6{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{2}^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{3} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3}.$

Question 7
?

Which curve is defined by the equation 3x12−6x1x2−5x22=24?

a
Two parallel lines
b
A hyperbola with semiaxes 6 and 4
c
An ellipse with semiaxes 6 and 2
d
An ellipse with semiaxes 6 and 4
e
A hyperbola with semiaxes 6 and 2
Submit

decision.explanation: The quadratic-form matrix [[3,−3],[−3,−5]] has characteristic polynomial λ²+2λ−24, so its eigenvalues are 4 and −6. In principal coordinates, 4y₁²−6y₂²=24 becomes y₁²/6−y₂²/4=1: a hyperbola with semiaxes √6 and 2.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $3{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}=24?$
after.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ -3 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-6\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $4{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2} & =24 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{6}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{6}$ and $2.$

a
Two parallel lines
b
A hyperbola with semiaxes 6 and 4
c
An ellipse with semiaxes 6 and 2
d
An ellipse with semiaxes 6 and 4
e
A hyperbola with semiaxes 6 and 2

Correct
EXPLANATION

Consider the quadratic form Q(x)=3x12−6x1x2−5x22. To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce Q(x) to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of Q(x), which is

A=[3−3−3−5].

Next, we find the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|3−λ−3−3−5−λ|=0λ2+2λ−24=0λ=4,−6

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to 4y12−6y22.

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

4y12−6y22=24y126−y224=1y12(6)2−y2222=1

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes 6 and 2.

Question 8
?

Which curve is defined by the equation −5x12+6x1x2+3x22=12?

a
Two parallel lines
b
An ellipse with semiaxes 3 and 4
c
A hyperbola with semiaxes 3 and 2
d
A hyperbola with semiaxes 3 and 4
e
A circle with radius 3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Consider the quadratic form Q(x)=−5x12+6x1x2+3x22. To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce Q(x) to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of Q(x), which is

A=[−5333].

Next, we find the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|−5−λ333−λ|=0λ2+2λ−24=0λ=4,−6

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to 4y12−6y22.

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

4y12−6y22=12y123−y222=1y12(3)2−y22(2)2=1

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes 3 and 2.

verification.explanation: The eigenvalues are 4 and −6, so the principal-axis equation is y₁²/3−y₂²/2=1. This confirms a hyperbola with semiaxes √3 and √2, matching the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback refers to the deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying a Quadratic Plane Curve
content.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $-5{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}=12?$
content.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=-5{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-6\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $4{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{2}.$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation ${x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=8?$
after.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $4{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2} & =8 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $2.$

b

A=[1331].

|A−λI|=0|1−λ331−λ|=0λ2−2λ−8=0λ=4,−2

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to 4y12−2y22.

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

4y12−2y22=8y122−y224=1y12(2)2−y2222=1

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes 2 and 2.

decision.explanation: The quadratic-form matrix [[2,−3],[−3,10]] has characteristic polynomial λ²−12λ+11, giving eigenvalues 1 and 11. In principal coordinates, y₁²+11y₂²=44 becomes y₁²/44+y₂²/4=1. This is an ellipse with semiaxes 2√11 and 2.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $2{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+10{x}_{2}^{2}=44?$
after.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+10{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +11 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =11,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $11{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}11{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} & =44 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{44} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{11})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $2$ and $2\sqrt{11}.$

Question 10
?

Which curve is defined by the equation 2x12−6x1x2+10x22=44?

a
An ellipse with semiaxes 2 and 211
b
A parabola
c
A hyperbola with semiaxes 1 and 11
d
A hyperbola with semiaxes 2 and 211
e
An ellipse with semiaxes 3 and 311
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Consider the quadratic form Q(x)=2x12−6x1x2+10x22. To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce Q(x) to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of Q(x), which is

A=[2−3−310].

Next, we find the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|2−λ−3−310−λ|=0λ2−12λ+11=0λ=11,1

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to 11y12+y22.

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

11y12+y22=44y124+y2244=1y1222+y22(211)2=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes 2 and 211.

before.html:
Question 11
?

Consider the matrix A=[−3335] and the quadratic curve xTAx=3. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=6 and λ2=−4, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
110[13] and 110[−31]
b
113[−23] and 113[32]
c
15[12] and 15[−21]
d
15[−23] and 15[32]
e
110[62] and 110[−26]
Submit

decision.explanation: Principal axes are orthonormal eigenvectors of A. Direct multiplication gives A(1,3)ᵀ=6(1,3)ᵀ and A(−3,1)ᵀ=−4(−3,1)ᵀ. These vectors are perpendicular and both have norm √10, so option a gives the normalized principal axes.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=3.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=3
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 11
?

Consider the matrix A=[−3335] and the quadratic curve xTAx=3. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=6 and λ2=−4, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
110[13] and 110[−31]
b
113[−23] and 113[32]
c
15[12] and 15[−21]
d
15[−23] and 15[32]
e
110[62] and 110[−26]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=3

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for A. Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=6, we have A−6I=[−3335]−6[1001]=[−933−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[13]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=10, we get v1‖v1‖=110[13].

  • For λ2=−4, we have A−(−4)I=[−3335]+4[1001]=[1339]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−4)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−31]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=10, we get v2‖v2‖=110[−31].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

110[13] and 110[−31].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues
content.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=3.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=3
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 12
?

Consider the matrix A=[−2221] and the quadratic curve xTAx=7. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=2 and λ2=−3, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
 110[31] and 110[−31]
b
 110[3−1] and 110[31]
c
113[32] and 113[−3−2]
d
 15[−21] and 15[−1−2]
e
 15[12] and 15[−21]
Submit

decision.explanation: A(1,2)ᵀ=2(1,2)ᵀ and A(−2,1)ᵀ=−3(−2,1)ᵀ. These eigenvectors are perpendicular and have norm √5, so option e gives normalized principal axes in the stated eigenvalue order. Option d represents the same axes with reversed order and a sign change.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=7.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=7
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 12
?

Consider the matrix A=[−2221] and the quadratic curve xTAx=7. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=2 and λ2=−3, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
 110[31] and 110[−31]
b
 110[3−1] and 110[31]
c
113[32] and 113[−3−2]
d
 15[−21] and 15[−1−2]
e
 15[12] and 15[−21]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=7

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for A. Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=2, we have A−2I=[−2221]−2[1001]=[−422−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[12]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[12].

  • For λ2=−3, we have A−(−3)I=[−2221]+3[1001]=[1224]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−3)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−21]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[−21].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

15[12] and 15[−21].

verification.explanation: The normalized eigenvectors are (1,2)ᵀ/√5 for eigenvalue 2 and (−2,1)ᵀ/√5 for eigenvalue −3, matching option e and the revealed solution. Option d describes the same axes with reversed order and a sign change. The incorrect submission was option b.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues
content.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=7.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=7
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Consider the matrix A=[5115] and the quadratic curve xTAx=2. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=6 and λ2=4, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
13[−21] and 13[21]
b
15[−34] and 15[34]
c
12[11] and 12[−11]
d
15[−21] and 15[21]
e
113[−23] and 113[23]
Submit

decision.explanation: A(1,1)ᵀ=6(1,1)ᵀ and A(−1,1)ᵀ=4(−1,1)ᵀ. These eigenvectors are perpendicular and each has norm √2, so dividing by √2 gives the principal axes in option c.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=2.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=2
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 13
?

Consider the matrix A=[5115] and the quadratic curve xTAx=2. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=6 and λ2=4, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
13[−21] and 13[21]
b
15[−34] and 15[34]
c
12[11] and 12[−11]
d
15[−21] and 15[21]
e
113[−23] and 113[23]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=2

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for A. Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For λ2=6, we have A−6I=[5115]−6[1001]=[−111−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[11]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[11].

  • For λ1=4, we have A−4I=[5115]−4[1001]=[1111]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[−11]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[−11].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

12[11] and 12[−11].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues
content.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=2.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=2
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 14
?

Consider the matrix A=[−222−2] and the quadratic curve xTAx=7. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=0 and λ2=−4, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
12[11] and 12[−11]
b
113[23] and 113[−32]
c
15[34] and 15[−43]
d
110[13] and 110[−31]
e
15[21] and 15[−12]
Submit

decision.explanation: A(1,1)ᵀ=0 and A(−1,1)ᵀ=−4(−1,1)ᵀ. These perpendicular eigenvectors each have norm √2, so option a gives the orthonormal principal directions. Although the equation has no real points because xᵀAx=−2(x₁−x₂)²≤0, these directions still diagonalize its quadratic form.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=7.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=7
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 14
?

Consider the matrix A=[−222−2] and the quadratic curve xTAx=7. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=0 and λ2=−4, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
12[11] and 12[−11]
b
113[23] and 113[−32]
c
15[34] and 15[−43]
d
110[13] and 110[−31]
e
15[21] and 15[−12]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=7

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for A. Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=0, we have A−0I=[−222−2]−0[1001]=[−222−2]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[11]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[11].

  • For λ2=−4, we have A−(−4)I=[−222−2]+4[1001]=[2222]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−11]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[−11].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

12[11] and 12[−11].

verification.explanation: Option a matches the revealed solution: (1,1)ᵀ/√2 and (−1,1)ᵀ/√2 are orthonormal eigenvectors for eigenvalues 0 and −4. They diagonalize the quadratic form, although its level set xᵀAx=7 has no real points. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option b.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues
content.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=7.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=7
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=3.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=3
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-7)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-7)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Question 15
?

Consider the matrix A=[2−3−3−6] and the quadratic curve xTAx=3. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=3 and λ2=−7, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
110[−31] and 110[13]
b
15[43] and 15[−34]
c
15[12] and 12[−21]
d
113[32] and 113[−23]
e
12[11] and 12[−11]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=3

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for A. Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=3, we have A−3I=[2−3−3−6]−3[1001]=[−1−3−3−9]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[−31]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=10, we get v1‖v1‖=110[−31].

  • For λ2=−7, we have A−(−7)I=[2−3−3−6]+7[1001]=[9−3−31]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−7)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[13]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=10, we get v2‖v2‖=110[13].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

110[−31] and 110[13].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues
content.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=3.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
content.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=3
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-7)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-7)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Question 16
?

Find the principal axes of the curve 9x12+8x1x2−6x22=5.

a
15[21] and 15[−12]
b
113[14] and 113[−41]
c
117[41] and 117[−14]
d
12[11] and 12[−11]
e
110[31] and 117[−13]
Submit

decision.explanation: The quadratic-form matrix is A=[[9,4],[4,−6]]. Direct multiplication gives A(4,1)ᵀ=10(4,1)ᵀ and A(−1,4)ᵀ=−7(−1,4)ᵀ. These eigenvectors are perpendicular and both have norm √17, so option c gives the orthonormal principal axes.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $9{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2}=5.$
after.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=9{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=5
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-7.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-7)I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}]+7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

Question 16
?

Find the principal axes of the curve 9x12+8x1x2−6x22=5.

a
15[21] and 15[−12]
b
113[14] and 113[−41]
c
117[41] and 117[−14]
d
12[11] and 12[−11]
e
110[31] and 117[−13]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, consider the quadratic form Q(x)=9x12+8x1x2−6x22. The matrix of the form is

A=[944−6].

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=5

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of A.

By solving the characteristic equation |A−λI|=0, we obtain

λ1=10 and λ2=−7.

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=10, we have A−10I=[944−6]−10[1001]=[−144−16]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−10I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[41]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=17, we get v1‖v1‖=117[41].

  • For λ2=−7, we have A−(−7)I=[944−6]+7[1001]=[16441]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−1I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−14]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=17, we get v2‖v2‖=117[−14].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

117[41] and 117[−14].

verification.explanation: For A=[[9,4],[4,−6]], A(4,1)ᵀ=10(4,1)ᵀ and A(−1,4)ᵀ=−7(−1,4)ᵀ. Both vectors have norm √17 and are perpendicular, confirming option c and the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option b.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve
content.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $9{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2}=5.$
content.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=9{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=5
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-7.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-7)I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}]+7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

Find the principal axes of the curve 24x12+4x1x2+21x22=100.

a
110[31] and 110[−13]
b
12[11] and 12[−11]
c
113[23] and 113[−32]
d
15[21] and 15[−12]
e
13[11] and 13[−11]
Submit

decision.explanation: The quadratic-form matrix is A=[[24,2],[2,21]]. A(2,1)ᵀ=25(2,1)ᵀ and A(−1,2)ᵀ=20(−1,2)ᵀ. These eigenvectors are perpendicular and both have norm √5, so option d gives the orthonormal principal axes.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}=100.$
after.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=100
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=25\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=20.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-25I & =[\begin{aligned}24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-25I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=20,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-20I & =[\begin{aligned}24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-20I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Question 17
?

Find the principal axes of the curve 24x12+4x1x2+21x22=100.

a
110[31] and 110[−13]
b
12[11] and 12[−11]
c
113[23] and 113[−32]
d
15[21] and 15[−12]
e
13[11] and 13[−11]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, consider the quadratic form Q(x)=24x12+4x1x2+21x22. The matrix of the form is

A=[242221].

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=100

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of A.

By solving the characteristic equation |A−λI|=0, we obtain

λ1=25 and λ2=20.

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=25, we have A−25I=[242221]−25[1001]=[−122−4]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−25I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[21]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[21].

  • For λ2=20, we have A−20I=[242221]−20[1001]=[4221]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−20I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−12]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[−12].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

15[21] and 15[−12].

content.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}=100.$
content.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=100
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

$$

$$

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=20,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-20I & =[\begin{aligned}24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

decision.explanation: The quadratic-form matrix is A=[[4,−2],[−2,1]]. A(−2,1)ᵀ=5(−2,1)ᵀ and A(1,2)ᵀ=0. These eigenvectors are perpendicular and both have norm √5, so option d gives the orthonormal principal axes.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $4{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=35.$
after.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=35
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=0.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

a

b
110[31] and 110[−13]

129[−25] and 129[52]

15[−21] and 15[12]
e
12[11] and 12[−11]

EXPLANATION

First, consider the quadratic form Q(x)=4x12−4x1x2+x22. The matrix of the form is

A=[4−2−21].

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=35

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of A.

By solving the characteristic equation |A−λI|=0, we obtain

λ1=5 and λ2=0.

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=5, we have A−5I=[4−2−21]−5[1001]=[−1−2−2−4]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[−21]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[−21].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[4−2−21]−0[1001]=[4−2−21]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[12]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[12].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

15[−21] and 15[12].

verification.explanation: For A=[[4,−2],[−2,1]], (−2,1)ᵀ and (1,2)ᵀ are eigenvectors for eigenvalues 5 and 0. They are perpendicular and each has norm √5, confirming option d and the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option c.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve
content.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $4{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=35.$
content.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=35
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=0.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

15[12] and 15[−21]

decision.explanation: The quadratic-form matrix is A=[[2,−2],[−2,2]]. A(−1,1)ᵀ=4(−1,1)ᵀ and A(1,1)ᵀ=0. These eigenvectors are perpendicular and each has norm √2, so option d gives the orthonormal principal axes.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$
after.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=9
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=4\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=0.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 19
?

Find the principal axes of the curve 2x12−4x1x2+2x22=9.

a
15[12] and 15[−21]
b
110[13] and 110[−31]
c
13[−21] and 13[12]
d
12[−11] and 12[11]
e
113[−32] and 113[23]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, consider the quadratic form Q(x)=2x12−4x1x2+2x22. The matrix of the form is

A=[2−2−22].

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=9

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of A.

By solving the characteristic equation |A−λI|=0, we obtain

λ1=4 and λ2=0.

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=4, we have A−4I=[2−2−22]−4[1001]=[−2−2−2−2]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[−11]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[−11].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[2−2−22]−0[1001]=[2−2−22]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[11]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[11].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

12[−11] and 12[11].

content.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$
content.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=9
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=4\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=0.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

decision.explanation: The quadratic-form matrix is A=[[4,12],[12,−3]]. A(4,3)ᵀ=13(4,3)ᵀ and A(−3,4)ᵀ=−12(−3,4)ᵀ. These eigenvectors are perpendicular and both have norm 5, so option b gives the orthonormal principal axes.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $4{x}_{1}^{2}+24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2}=72.$
after.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 12 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=1
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=13\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-12.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=13,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-13I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 12 & -3\end{aligned}]-13[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-13I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=5,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-12,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-12)I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 12 & -3\end{aligned}]+12[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-12)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=5,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

Question 20

Find the principal axes of the curve 4x12+24x1x2−3x22=72.

a
15[21] and 15[−12]
b
15[43] and 15[−34]
c
113[23] and 113[−32]
d
110[13] and 110[−31]
e
117[41] and 117[−14]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, consider the quadratic form Q(x)=4x12+24x1x2−3x22. The matrix of the form is

A=[41212−3].

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=1

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of A.

By solving the characteristic equation |A−λI|=0, we obtain

λ1=13 and λ2=−12.

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=13, we have A−13I=[41212−3]−13[1001]=[−91212−16]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−13I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[43]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[43].

  • For λ2=−12, we have A−(−12)I=[41212−3]+12[1001]=[1612129]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−12)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−34]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[−34].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

15[43] and 15[−34].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve
content.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $4{x}_{1}^{2}+24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2}=72.$
content.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 12 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=1
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=13\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-12.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=13,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-13I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 12 & -3\end{aligned}]-13[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-13I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=5,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-12,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-12)I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 12 & -3\end{aligned}]+12[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-12)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=5,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$
